newsitem.title: USA: U.S. cautiously welcomes Serbia election move.
newsitem.headline: U.S. cautiously welcomes Serbia election move.

text.p: The United States cautiously welcomed a decision by Serbia's president to reinstate local election results on Tuesday but said it would remain sceptical until the opposition took its seats in city councils.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said that if the Belgrade announcement of President Slobodan Milosevic's action turned out to be accurate, "we welcome this as a first step forward in the right direction in Serbia."
Speaking to a regular State Department briefing, Burns added: "However, we will remain sceptical until we see concrete actions by the Serbian government to implement the commitment made this morning.
"We need to see concrete actions that demonstrate in deed that the Serbian government will recognise and respect the results of the November 17 elections," he said.
"And that means that the people who won the elections...will actually take their seats in the city councils all over Serbia and begin to govern."

Milosevic, making a sudden climbdown in the face of 11 weeks of pro-democracy demonstrations, said in Belgrade that the victories by the Zajedno opposition coalition, which had been annulled by the courts, must be reinstated.
The authoritarian leader, who had virtually ignored the street unrest buffeting the country and unleashed police on demonstrators two days ago, asked parliament to restore the election outcome.
Zajedno had claimed victory in 14 cities and towns, including Belgrade. Their victory was confirmed by a mission from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe.
Burns said the United States and other Western powers were demanding that there be no further use of police force against demonstrators.
"The people have a right to be in the streets to demonstrate for their basic political rights," he said.
He said it would be unacceptable for Milosevic's Socialists to cede the election results only to then strip away local council powers, including control of local media.
"If the Serbian government is going to play games here...that would not be fair play. And that would not be accepted by the rest of the world," he said.
